rule: Je suis is how you say who you are, and tu es is how you say who someone you know well is. C'est points at someone or something. Every noun is masculine or feminine: un goes with a masculine noun (un homme, un garçon), une with a feminine one (une femme, une fille).

Le, la, l' and les come before a noun when you mean a particular one. Le goes with a masculine noun (le livre), la with a feminine one (la lettre), l' before a vowel (l'homme), and les with more than one (les enfants). Il est and elle est are for one person or thing; ils sont and elles sont for more than one.

Tu is for one person you know well, a friend or a child. Vous is for someone you don't know, someone you're polite to, or more than one person: vous êtes instead of tu es. Polite phrases follow the same choice: s'il te plaît with tu, s'il vous plaît with vous.

A verb that ends in -er, like manger and aimer, changes its ending to match who is doing it: je mange, tu manges, il mange. Je becomes j' before a vowel: j'aime. Du goes before a masculine noun when you mean some of it: du pain.
Avoir doesn't follow the -er pattern; each form has to be learned: j'ai, tu as, il a. Il a and il est sound close and are easy to mix up, so listen for the difference.

For more than one, les means the and des means some. English often leaves des out: j'ai des livres is I have books. Most nouns add an s you can't hear (un chat, des chats). Nouns ending in -eau add an x (un oiseau, des oiseaux), and most ending in -al change to -aux (un cheval, des chevaux). Nous sommes is we are.

A describing word takes the noun's gender. Many add -e for a feminine noun: bon, bonne; gentil, gentille. A few change more: beau becomes belle, and vieux becomes vieille. Most describing words come after the noun, but short everyday ones like beau, jeune, vieux, bon, petit and grand come before it: un beau jeune homme. Très in front means very.

Mon, ton and son mean my, your and his or her. They match the thing owned, not the owner: mon livre, ma pomme, mes livres. Son ami can mean his friend or her friend; French doesn't say which. Before a feminine word that starts with a vowel, mon is used instead of ma: mon amie.

The simplest question is a sentence said with a rising voice: tu as un chien ? Est-ce que at the start makes a yes-or-no question without changing the sentence. Qu'est-ce que asks what, qui asks who, où asks where, and pourquoi asks why; parce que answers it. Quel goes with a masculine noun and quelle with a feminine one: quel livre, quelle pomme.

Numbers come before the noun, and the noun is plural from two on: deux chats, trois enfants. Combien de asks how many: tu as combien de chats ? To say how many people are in a group, French says nous sommes trois, there are three of us.

Colours come after the noun and match it: un chat noir, une souris noire. Vert, noir and bleu add -e for a feminine noun; blanc becomes blanche. Rouge and jaune already end in -e, so they stay the same.

Time words often go at the start or the end of the sentence: aujourd'hui, c'est lundi. Le matin and le soir mean in the morning and in the evening. Days of the week have no capital letter in French. The present tense is used for plans too: je suis ici demain.
Aller, to go, has its own forms: je vais, tu vas, il va. À means to or at. À and le join to make au: je vais au parc, but je vais à l'école. Dans means in or inside.

Three phrases keep a conversation going when you're lost. Je ne comprends pas: I don't understand (ne … pas wraps the verb to say not). Plus lentement, s'il vous plaît: more slowly, please. Répétez, s'il vous plaît: please repeat. Use the vous forms (parlez, répétez) with someone you don't know, the tu forms (parle, répète) with a friend.

Two questions get you a word you don't know. Qu'est-ce que ça veut dire ? asks what something means (vouloir dire, literally to want to say, is to mean): Non veut dire non. Comment on dit … en français ? asks how to say something: on is one or people, and dit is says. Français and anglais name the languages, with no capital letter.

When the word won't come, talk around it. Je cherche le mot: I'm looking for the word. C'est une chose pour l'eau: it's a thing for water (pour is for). Comment ça s'appelle ? asks what something is called (s'appeler, to be called). And Je ne sais pas, I don't know, is always allowed.

To give your name, French uses s'appeler, to be called: je m'appelle Paul, tu t'appelles, vous vous appelez. The me, te or vous before the verb is part of it (m' and t' before a vowel). To ask, say Comment tu t'appelles ? to a friend, Vous vous appelez comment ? politely, or Quel est votre nom ? Your nom is your family name; your prénom is your first name.

Two ways to get a word or a name spelled. Comment ça s'écrit ? asks how it's written. Vous pouvez épeler ? asks someone to spell it (pouvoir, can: je peux, tu peux, vous pouvez, then the verb as it is: épeler, écrire). The answer comes letter by letter: P, A, U, L.

French phone numbers have ten digits, read in pairs: 06 11 15 19 20 is zéro six, onze, quinze, dix-neuf, vingt. From eleven to sixteen each number has its own word (onze, douze, treize, quatorze, quinze, seize); seventeen to nineteen are ten and seven, ten and eight, ten and nine, with hyphens (dix-sept, dix-huit, dix-neuf). Quel est ton numéro ? asks someone's number.

French gives your age with avoir, to have: J'ai vingt ans is I am twenty (literally I have twenty years). Quel est ton âge ? asks it. Né and née mean born, with être: il est né ici, elle est née ici (née for a woman). Bon anniversaire ! is happy birthday.

Numbers go by fast, so check them. Pardon, vous pouvez répéter ? asks for it again (pouvoir plus the verb as it is). Un moment, s'il vous plaît, or Attendez un moment, buys you time. Je vais noter says you'll write it down: je vais plus a verb is what you're about to do.

The tens: trente (30), quarante (40), cinquante (50), soixante (60). Then French counts on from sixty: soixante-dix is sixty-ten (70), quatre-vingts is four twenties (80), quatre-vingt-dix is four twenties and ten (90), and cent is a hundred. Ages take avoir: elle a soixante ans.

J'habite means I live: habiter goes like parler (j'habite, tu habites, il habite, vous habitez). Tu habites où ? asks where. A French address puts the number first, then the street: dix, rue du Parc. Près de is near, loin de far from; de and le make du (près du parc).

Countries take en for in and to: j'habite en France, je vais en Italie. Nationalities and languages share a word, with no capital letter: il est allemand (German, the person), je parle allemand (the language). For a woman, most add -e: elle est allemande. Une langue is a language.

Je voudrais is the polite way to ask for something: I would like (from vouloir: je veux is I want, je voudrais is softer). A quantity takes de: un kilo de pommes. Acheter, to buy, adds an accent in j'achète, tu achètes, il achète. Des fruits, des légumes: des is some, for more than one.

Say when you've understood, and check that you have. J'ai compris: I understood (compris is the past of comprendre). Tu as compris ? asks. D'accord means OK, agreed: je suis d'accord, I agree. C'est vrai ? Is that true? And exactement, exactly, confirms.

Ça coûte combien ? or Combien ça coûte ? asks the price. Coûter goes like parler: ça coûte (it costs), ils coûtent (they cost). French says the euros first, then the cents: trois euros cinquante is 3,50 €, with a comma for the decimal point. Cher means expensive (and, before a name, dear): c'est cher, la pomme est chère.

A quantity takes de, or d' before a vowel: une bouteille d'eau, un paquet de fromage, un verre de lait. The same goes for beaucoup de, peu de, assez de and trop de: beaucoup d'argent, a lot of money. Trop is too or too much: c'est trop cher.
